<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely narrow, well-shaped clash. B (PRO) built a clean three-part case (informed consent, surveillance pricing as categorically distinct, cheap-disclosure asymmetry) and drew a usable line — transaction features versus inferred personal profile — then landed its single best blow in closing: A's "second tab / marginal shopper" discipline presupposes that firms cannot separate the vigilant from the inattentive, which is exactly the separation personalization is built to achieve. That materially damaged one of A's prongs. But A (CON) did more comparative work across the whole exchange and left two pressures unresolved for B. First, A forced B into a dilemma after B4.1: if disclosure only means admitting "personalization is happening," it is a cookie banner that changes no price for the midnight shopper; if it means publishing differentials, it triggers A's leveling-up mechanism. B's closing pivoted to the mechanism argument and never resolved that dilemma. Second, A repeatedly showed that B's own paradigm villain — the desperate late-night buyer facing few local sellers — is priced on time and local competition, i.e. transaction features, and therefore permitted under B's line. B never answered that, so A's "scalpel held backwards" charge survived. B's best counter (student/senior/loyalty discounts have been disclosed for decades and were not killed) was well chosen, but A turned it plausibly by distinguishing legible moral categories from churn-risk pricing and pointing to loyalty-penalty compression where new-customer prices rose. Both openings were clipped for length, a shared execution cost. A also answered pressure questions with crisp, properly labelled, non-evasive A1/A2 responses. On balance A made the decision easier: it gave a reason why the rule as written misses the abuse and taxes the discount, and offered a concrete narrower alternative.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B4.1: once B conceded the retention coupon survives and disclosure means only that firms "can't hide that personalization is happening," A's [A4.3]-[A4.4] reduced the mandate to a cookie banner — toothless if narrow, discount-killing if it has bite — and B's closing never resolved that dilemma, instead changing ground to the marginal-shopper mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
